PREPARED BY:  Kelly Ribuffo, Contract Planner  APP TYPE(S): SPR, CUP, CDP___

SUBJECT:  A Public Hearing considering a Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and
  Coastal Development Permit to allow the conversion of six bedrooms into
  six individual hotel rooms in the Annex building at Mt. Ada and parking
  improvements at 207 Wrigley Road (PC#2917)
________________________________________________________________________

SUMMARY: A Public Hearing considering a Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and Coastal
Development Permit to allow conversion of the Annex building at Mt. Ada from six bedrooms to
six individual hotel rooms and associated parking improvements in the Resort Recreation (R/R)
zone. The Proposed Project is categorically exempt from the California Environmental Quality
Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15303 (Class 3 – New Construction or Conversion of
Small Structures). The proposed project is not located within the appealable area of the Coastal
Zone.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S):

  1. Conduct a public hearing;

  2. Find this project exempt from the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) pursuant
  to Section 15303 under Class 3 (New Construction or Conversion of Small Structures) of
  the CEQA Guidelines, because the conversion of six bedrooms to hotel rooms and
  associated parking improvements has no potential to have a significant effect on the
  environment; and

  3. Adopt Resolution No. PC 26-13 approving a Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and
  Coastal Development Permit pursuant to PC#2917 (Attachment 1).

AUTHORIZING GUIDELINES: Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Sections 9-8.401, 9-8.203.a, and
9-8.103.a authorize the Planning Commission to review and take action on applications for a
Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and Coastal Development Permit.

BACKGROUND:

Application Information:

  Applicant  Jason Chung, Representative
  Owner  Santa Catalina Island Company
  Location  207 Wrigley Road (Wrigley Terrace Road)
  APN  7480-004-007
  General Plan  Resort Recreational – High Density
  Land Use Designation
  Zoning Classification  Resort Recreation (R/R)
  File Date  7/2/2026
   PC#2917 – Mt. Ada Annex
  Page 2

Existing Site and Area Context:

The project site is located on a rectangular parcel (APN 7480-004-007) addressed 207 Wrigley
Road (Wrigley Terrace Road). Alternate addresses also include 398 Wrigley Road. The parcel
is situated at the peak of Mt. Ada, with sloping hillsides in all directions, with panoramic views to
the city center, Avalon Bay, and the San Pedro Channel.

Mt. Ada was constructed in 1921 for William Wrigley Jr. and his family as a private residence.
The property consists of three primary buildings – the main residence, Annex (Servant’s
Quarters), and detached garage. All three buildings are considered to be contributing historic
buildings to the property, which was listed to the National Register of Historic Places in 1985 for
its architecture and landscape architecture. By virtue of its listing in the National Register, Mt.
Ada was automatically listed in the California Register of Historical Resources when the
California Register was created in 1992.

The property functioned as a private residence until 1958, which the Santa Catalina Island
Company (Island Company) opened the property for public viewing after the death of William
Wrigley Jr. The property was donated to the University of Southern California in 1978. The
property was later returned to the Island Company in 2014, at which time operations were
transitioned to a hotel.
   PC#2917 – Mt. Ada Annex
  Page 3

The Annex building has not been used as full-time employee housing since the Island Company
took back the operation of the property in 2014. It was intermittently used for summer intern
accommodation until 2018, after which it has been used for back-of-house storage for the hotel.

All abutting properties are zoned Low Density Residential and Low Intensity Recreation (LD) or
Multiple Residential, Medium Density (MD) and represent a mix vacant parcels and multi-story
residential buildings. A vicinity map, showing adjacent property addresses and zoning, is
provided as Attachment 2 of this report.

Entitlement and Permit History:

The following active building permit has been granted for the project site:

  •  Building Permit #26137 – Approval of interior demolition of the Annex building. (July 2022)
  Demolition of building interiors does not require discretionary approval.

PROJECT DESCRIPTION: The applicant proposes an interior remodel and exterior remodel of
the Mt. Ada Annex building to convert it from a six bedrooms to a six hotel room expansion of
the existing hotel operations at Mt. Ada (aka Inn at Mt. Ada). Notable features of the project
include:

  •  Reconfiguration of interior floor plan from six bedrooms to six hotel rooms.

  •  Remove covered entrance on north elevation and construct new covered entry porticos
  on the south/southwest and east elevations.

  •  Restore existing historic windows or replace with compatible traditional wood window of
  similar pattern if needed.

  •  Replace existing non-historic exterior entry doors with new six-panel Georgian style doors
  with traditional metal lockset.

  •  Relocate six existing autoette parking spaces for guest vehicles from the north side of the
  Annex building to the east side and relandscape the previous parking area for passive
  garden space.

  •  Create new parking area for seven autoette parking spaces for guest amenity vehicles
  and two service vehicles to the east of the Annex building.

  •  Install new accessible walkways around the central vehicle roundabout from the Annex
  building to the main residence, with new wood deck at the south end of the walkway.

The proposed project plans are included as Attachment 3 of this report. No work is proposed
to the main residence or detached garage on the property as part of this project.

The proposed was evaluated for compliance pursuant to the development standards set forth in
Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) Section 9-6.404 for the R/R zoning district. It was determined that
the proposed improvements do not involve any changes that are restricted for development
standards for lot coverage, floor area, height, or setbacks. Most work proposed to the Annex
   PC#2917 – Mt. Ada Annex
  Page 4

building itself is located within the interior of the existing building envelope. The proposed entry
portico on the south/southwest elevation does not count towards floor area per the definition set
forth in AMC Section 9-3.606, as it is an open-sided structure, and is located hundreds of feet
from the nearest property line, well beyond required setbacks for the zone. Similarly, the
proposed parking improvements is located well within the boundaries of the parcel and does not
conflict with setbacks.

Design of off-street parking areas must comply with the standards set forth in AMC Section 9-
7.606 and 9-7.607.

  Table 1: Development Standards – Parking
  Required  Proposed
  Parking Space - Autoette  6 ft x 10 ft  6 ft x 10 ft
  Parking Space – Full-size 8 ft x 17 ft  10 ft x 18 ft and 10 ft x 22 ft
  Driveway Width  8 ft, one way  16 ft, two way
  Turnaround Area  Required if 100+ ft from Provided
  right-of-way
  Paving  Concrete or Asphalt  Concrete
  Marked Spaces  Required  Provided
  Landscaping  Required  Provided

The project must comply with standards for hotel room size per AMC Section 9-7.901, Hotel
Density. The proposed hotel rooms range in size from 232 to 761 square feet, which exceeds
the minimum hotel room size requirement of 190 square feet.

  Table 2: Development Standards – Hotel Room Size
  Required (sq. ft)  Proposed (sq. ft)
  Hotel Room Size*  190  232 to 761
  Bathroom Size**  >/= 35  66 to 155
* Total including en-suite bathroom
** Must include a sink, toilet, and shower stall.

Construction Phasing

The site will be developed over two phases based on the Southern California Edison (SCE)
water allotment for the property. SCE has provided a water allocation request letter (Attachment
4) confirming a sufficient existing fresh water allotment is available for the buildout of three hotel
rooms. The applicant is currently on the wait list for the remaining three hotel rooms. All hotel
rooms will be double occupancy in accordance with the SCE water allotment standards.

Phase 1

  •  Demolition of interior building areas and exterior porch.

  •  Develop first floor interior which will consist of three hotel rooms (Rooms 7-9).

  •  Relocate six autoette parking spaces to new location.
   PC#2917 – Mt. Ada Annex
  Page 5

Safety and security measures will be built as part of Phase 1 to protect the building until Phase
2 construction can commence. During Phase 1, the second-floor hotel rooms (Rooms 10-12) will
be completed up to rough framing, rough plumbing, rough electrical, and functional fire sprinklers
only.

Phase 2

  •  Finish interior buildout of three hotel rooms (Rooms 10-12) on the second floor.

DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS:

Issue 1: Mt. Ada as a Historic Resource
Mt. Ada (William Wrigley Jr. Cottage) was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in
1985 and automatically listed in the California Register of Historical Resources in 1992. The
Annex building is considered a contributing historic building on the property, though is
considered of secondary importance compared to the main residence.

Though the property has National Register recognition and is generally recognized as an
important historic site by residents, the City of Avalon does not have a historic preservation
ordinance to regulate alterations to historic resources within the community. Therefore,
alterations to the property can only be reviewed for compliance pursuant to the following
regulations:

  •  Site Plan review findings for compatibility with surrounding development and functional
  development design, as set forth in AMC Section 9-8.203; and

  •  Consideration as a qualified historic resource pursuant to CEQA to avoid substantial
  adverse changes in the significance of a historic resource for projects that require
  discretionary review.

Best practice for reviewing alterations to historic resources is to evaluate projects based on the
Secretary of the Interior’s Standards, published by the National Park Service, informed by the
historic features of the property as defined in the associate historic nomination or description.
Therefore, staff requested that the applicant hire a qualified historic preservation consultant to
prepare a character-defining features report to guide the design of the proposed project. This
report, prepared by Historic Resources Group (HRG) is included as Attachment 5.

The project proposes removal of an existing covered porch entrance on the north elevation which
is labeled as a “primary” character defining feature in HRG’s report, and creation of a new
entrance on the opposite façade. Generally, the Secretary of the Interior’s Standards for
Rehabilitation recommends avoiding removal of historic materials or alteration of features and
spaces that characterize a property. However, such changes can still be allowable so long as
their material, mass, scale, and design are compatible with the historic structure, do not
significantly dimmish the historic integrity of the resource, and allow for appropriate use or reuse
of a historic building.

It is the opinion of staff that the proposed alterations to the entrances of the Annex building do
not result in a significant adverse impact to the historic integrity of the Annex building or Mt. Ada
as a whole. The Annex will be repurposed from a former servant’s quarter’s/storage building to
an extension of the hotel operations in the main residence, which required minimal alterations
   PC#2917 – Mt. Ada Annex
  Page 6

to the exterior architectural features of the building, which is the basis for the significance of the
building in the National Register nomination. While the existing covered porch is identified as a
primary character defining feature, its removal does not constitute a significant impact to the
architectural design, material, and craftsmanship of the building or Mt. Ada as a whole, as it is
one feature within the context of a much larger property. Other proposed exterior improvements
are compatible with the Georgian architectural style of the building. Furthermore, the change in
the orientation of the main entrance to the building promotes efficient operations of the hotel, as
all guest buildings will now face the central courtyard/drop off area, limiting the potential for
operations to impose (via noise, light, etc.) on surrounding residential properties down the
hillside in the Terraces.

Therefore, staff recommends that findings for approval of the project can be made for both the
City’s Site Plan review criteria, and to allow a categorical exemption from CEQA, as outlined in
the draft resolution included as Attachment 1.

Issue 2: Parking
Per AMC Section 9-7.605, parking requirements for Parking for business uses may be set by
the Planning Commission. The property provides 6 autoette parking spaces (for vehicles that
are provided by the operator as an amenity to guests staying at the hotel) and an unmarked
loading zone on the east side of the property adjacent to the driveway access to the nearby
Verizon Wireless installation. Shuttle drop off at the interior driveway roundabout. Guests are
dropped off via hotel shuttle or local taxi services. No private guest vehicles are permitted to
park on-site. All staff are transported to the property via shuttle for work.

The applicant proposes removal of six existing autoette parking spaces from the north side of
the Annex building and the creation of a new parking area to the east side of the Annex building,
between the Annex and carriage house. The paved parking area will include seven autoette
parking spaces for guest amenity vehicles (6 ft x 10 ft) and two hotel service vehicles (10 ft x 22
ft). A new hotel shuttle parking space (10 ft x 18 ft) will be created along the existing driveway
roundabout. The existing loading zone will remain. The work will result in a net increase of four
marked parking spaces on the property.

It is the opinion of staff that it is unlikely that addition of new hotel rooms to Mt. Ada will increase
demand for on or off-street parking on the property. Guests and hotel employees are transported
to the property via shuttle or taxi service. The site provides dedicated vehicle parking spaces for
autoettes that are offered as an amenity to guests, therefore there is minimal potential for any
overflow parking onto Wrigley Road. Therefore, parking demand generated by hotel operations
will continue to be accommodated via off-street parking areas within the property.

Issue 3: Unit Conversion

The City has also considered the residential replacement requirements of the Housing Crisis Act
of 2019 (Gov. Code § 66300 et seq.). The Annex historically contained six bedrooms associated
with former servant/employee accommodations. City and Applicant records indicate that the
Annex has not been used as full-time employee housing since 2014, was used intermittently for
summer-intern accommodations until 2018, and has thereafter been used for hotel storage.

Government Code Section 66300.6(a) imposes a residential replacement requirement when a
housing development project demolishes residential dwelling units. As the proposed Project is
not a housing development project, this subdivision does not apply to this hotel project.
   PC#2917 – Mt. Ada Annex
  Page 7

Subdivision (b) imposes a replacement requirement for protected units, as defined in
Government Code Section 66300.5. A “protected unit” means: (1) Residential dwelling units that
are or were subject to a recorded covenant, ordinance, or law that restricts rents to levels
affordable to persons or families of lower or very low income within the past five years, (2)
Residential dwelling units that are or were subject to any form of rent or price control through a
public entity’s valid exercise of its police power within the past five years, (3) Residential dwelling
units that are or were rented by lower or very low income households within the past five years,
or (4) Residential dwelling units that were withdrawn from rent or lease in accordance with the
Ellis Act (Chapter 12.75 of Division 7 of Title 1) within the past ten years. Staff has evaluated
whether the units are protected units and determined that the bedrooms do not meet any of the
criteria such that these are protected units. Accordingly, the Project is not required to replace
the converted units under Government Code Section 66300.6.

GENERAL PLAN, LAND USE, AND ZONING COMPLIANCE:

Pursuant AMC Sections 9-8.404, 9-8.203, and 9-8.103.d, recommended findings for approval of
a Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and Coastal Development Permit are provided in draft
Resolution No. PC 26-13 (Attachment 1).

Annual Growth Policy

The growth policy provides that new residential or commercial development should only be
permitted with confirmation from Southern California Edison Company (“SCE”) that adequate
fresh water is available. On May 15, 2026, SCE issued a fresh water allocation letter stating that
fresh water is available for Phase 1 of the project (three hotel rooms) and that the project has
been placed on the fresh water wait list for Phase 2 (three additional hotel rooms). Therefore,
SCE has confirmed adequate fresh water is available to allow construction of Phase 1 of the
Project. Condition #3 of draft Resolution 26-13 requires that written confirmation of water
allocation status prior to issuance of any construction permits for Phase 2 of the Project.
Therefore, staff recommends that the Planning Commission makes the finding that the proposed
project is in compliance with the 2026 Annual Growth Policy.

ENVIRONMENTAL DETERMINATION: The proposed project is categorically exempt from the
provisions of the California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines
15303 (Class 3 – New Construction or Conversion of Small Structures) because it has no
potential to have a significant effect on the environment.

The Class 3 exemption includes the conversion of existing small structures from one use to
another where only minor modifications are made to the exterior of the structure. The project
involves conversion of an existing two-story building (Mt. Ada Annex) from six bedrooms to six
individual hotel rooms, with minor modifications to the exterior of the building to restore historic
features, add an architecturally compatible new entrance portico, and relocate existing autoette
parking spaces and develop new parking improvements within the existing developed area of
the site. As such, the project is not expected to have a significant environmental impact on the
surrounding area.

The project was evaluated pursuant to the criteria for the exceptions to the exemptions as
identified in Guidelines Section 14 CCR, Chapter 3, Article 19, Section 15300.2 and the Planning
Commission finds that there are no exceptions to the use of an exemption for the project. The
project does not impact an environmental resource of hazardous or critical concern, does not
   PC#2917 – Mt. Ada Annex
  Page 8

result in cumulative impacts, does not have a significant effect on the environment due to
unusual circumstances, does not damage scenic resources within a state scenic highway, and
is not a hazardous waste site.

Furthermore, Mt. Ada (William Wrigley Jr. Cottage), inclusive of the Annex building, was listed
on the National Register of Historic Places in 1985. The proposed changes to the building have
been designed with consideration for the character-defining features of the Annex building and
will not cause a substantial adverse change in the historic significance of the property.

ADVERTISING, NOTICE AND PUBLIC CONTACT: August 7, 2026, the City sent a Public
Hearing Notice to owners/tenants within a 300-foot radius of the project site. The Hearing Notice
was published in Catalina Islander on August 7, 2026. The notice was posted in two additional
locations on the same date.

  LOCATED AT 207 WRIGLEY ROAD (PC#2917)

  WHEREAS, Jason Chung, representing the Santa Catalina Island Company (“Applicant”)
filed an application (“Application”) for a Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and Coastal
Development Permit (PC#2917) to approve the conversion of six bedroom into six individual hotel
rooms in the Annex building at Mt. Ada and associated parking improvements (“Project”) on the
property located at 207 Wrigley Road, APN 7480-004-007 (“Site”); and

  WHEREAS, the Planning Commission has authority per Avalon Municipal Code (AMC)
Sections 9-8.401, 9-8.203.a, and 9-8.103.a to review and take action on the subject applications
for a Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and Coastal Development Permit; and

  WHEREAS, the Site is categorized Resort Recreational – High Density by the General
Plan Land Use Element and is located within the designated area of the Resort Recreation (R/R)
zoning district; and

  WHEREAS, the Site is located within the Coastal Zone and is within the planning
boundaries of the Avalon Local Coastal Program; and

  WHEREAS, the Project was found to be categorically exempt from CEQA per State
CEQA Guidelines 15303 (Class 3 – New Construction or Conversion of Small Structures). No
public review is required; and
  WHEREAS, the City has considered the Housing Crisis Act of 2019, Government Code
section 66300 et seq., including the residential-unit replacement requirements of Government
Code section 66300.6, and finds, based on the administrative records, that the six bedrooms in the
Annex building at Mt. Ada have not been used for residential occupancy since 2018, and none of
the bedrooms within the Annex constitutes a “protected unit” within the meaning of Government
Code section 66300.5. None of the units have been subject to an affordability restriction, rent or
price control, or rented by lower or very-low-income households within the last five years, and
none of the units were withdrawn under the Ellis Act within the last ten years. (See Gov. Code §
66300.5(h)) Accordingly, the replacement requirements of Government Code section 66300.6(b)
do not require replacement housing in connection with the Project; and
  WHEREAS, the Planning Commission conducted one duly advertised public hearing on
August 19, 2026, at which time interested persons had an opportunity to testify either in support
of or opposition to granting a Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and Coastal Development Permit
upon property described in attached Exhibit “A”; and

  1
   WHEREAS, all other legal prerequisites for the consideration of the Conditional Use
Permit, Site Plan, and Coastal Development Permit have occurred.

  NOW, THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that the Planning Commission of the City of
Avalon does hereby approve a Conditional Use Permit, Site Plan, and Coastal Development Permit
for the conversion of six bedrooms into six individual hotel rooms in the Annex building at Mt.
Ada and associated parking improvements, located at 207 Wrigley Road, based on the following
findings:

SECTION 1 – ENVIRONMENTAL REVIEW
The proposed Project is categorically exempt from the provisions of the California Environmental
Quality Act (CEQA) per State CEQA Guidelines 15303 (Class 3 – New Construction or
Conversion of Small Structures) because it has no potential to have a significant effect on the
environment.

The Class 3 exemption includes the conversion of existing small structures from one use to another
where only minor modifications are made to the exterior of the structure. The project involves
conversion of an existing two-story building (Mt. Ada Annex) from six bedrooms to six individual
hotel rooms, with minor modifications to the exterior of the building to restore historic features,
add an architecturally compatible new entrance portico, and develop new parking improvements
within the existing developed area of the site. As such, the project is not expected to have a
significant environmental impact on the surrounding area.

 1.0 INTRODUCTION
HRG has identified extant and visible exterior character-defining features of the Mt. Ada Annex
located at 398 Wrigley Road in the City of Avalon, Santa Catalina Island, California. The

 2.0 HISTORIC SIGNIFICANCE
Historic significance is defined by the National Park Service as “the importance of a property to
the history, architecture, archaeology, engineering, or culture of a community, state, or the
nation.”1 Historic significance is achieved by association with important events, activities, or
patterns; association with important persons; distinctive physical characteristics of design,
construction, or form; or potential to yield important information. 2

The William Wrigley, Jr. Summer Cottage, more commonly known as Mt. Ada, is listed in the
National Register of Historic Places (1985) and the California Register of Historical Resources
(1992). The “National Register of Historic Places Inventory-Nomination Form” submitted for
the National Register listing does not specifically identify the National Register criterion or
criteria under which Mt. Ada is significant; however, the form identifies the Areas of
Significance as “architecture” and “landscape architecture,” with a specific period of significance
of 1921. This indicates that the property is significant under Criterion C. The Statement of
Significance states:

  The Wrigley Summer Cottage or “Mt. Ada” is significant for its architectural quality and
  integrity, and as the finest residential and garden complex ever constructed on Santa
  Catalina Island. The estate is historically significant as having been the vacation residence
  of Mr. and Mrs. William Wrigley Jr. of Chicago, founders of the vast Wrigley chewing gum
  fortune and recognized as one of the world’s wealthiest families. As a result of Mr.
  Wrigley’s great political influence, Mt. Ada was frequently visited by Presidents Calvin
  Coolidge and Herbert Hoover, subsequently becoming known as the “Summer White
  House.” An adjacent portion of the estate was sculpted into a baseball playing field 3 which
  received nationwide attention as the spring training camp of the Chicago Cubs. Mt. Ada is
  further significant for its design and quality of construction. It is associated with the
  following prominent firms and individuals: The Santa Catalina Island Company, chief
  architect David M. Renton, engineer Capt. A. B. Waddingham, and landscape architect
  Albert Conrad. Mt. Ada is the finest extant residential structure designed by architect
  Renton. The estate is situated atop the most desirable viewing location on the island,
  approximately 350 feet above sea level. Mt. Ada serves the community as a local landmark;
  it is visually prominent from most points in the City of Avalon as well as Avalon Bay – main
  point of entry to Santa Catalina Island. The estate is well known to the public. It was fully
  documented in most current tourism literature covering Santa Catalin Island. The Santa
  Catalina Island Company opened Mt. Ada for public viewing shortly after the death of Mrs.
  William Wrigley Jr. in 1958 until its donation to the University of Southern California in
  1978. The main residence and servant’s [sic.] quarters have remained virtually unaltered,
  however the garage has been significantly altered as a result of conversion to living
  quarters. The Wrigley Summer Cottage retains a powerful sense of historical and
  architectural time and place unique to Santa Catalina Island.4

 3.0 PHYSICAL DESCRIPTION
Architectural Description
The William Wrigley Jr. Summer Cottage complex consists of three buildings and various
landscape features on a hilltop above Avalon Harbor. The parcel occupied by the Cottage
complex is wrapped on two sides by a sharp bend in Wrigley Road, from which it is accessed by
a sloping driveway that terminates in a circular motor court. The northwest and northeast sides
of the motor court are enclosed by the Main Residence, a two-story, Neoclassical style building
with an L-shaped plan. A porte-cochère with Doric columns, entablature, and balustrade spans
the driveway and connects the northeast wing of the Main Residence to the Annex, formerly
servants’ quarters, which is located on the southeast side of the motor court. The garage is
located southeast of the Annex.

The Annex is a two-story Neoclassical style building with a roughly rectangular plan, simple
massing, and asymmetrical composition. It has a moderately-pitched hipped roof with boxed
eaves, a continuous eave cornice, and a pedimented dormer above the northeast façade. There
is a second-story polygonal oriel at the northeast corner, with a conical roof and turned spire.
An angled projection on the northwest façade, which receives the porte-cochère, has a flat roof.
The exterior walls are veneered in smooth cement plaster. The northwest façade is articulated
at the second-floor level by a continuation of the porte-cochère’s entablature. Fenestration
consists primarily of six-over-one double-hung wood sash windows with wood stucco molds,
projecting wood sills, and louvered wood shutters. Some windows are coupled. There are two
pairs of divided light, wood French doors on the southwest façade, one with sidelights.

There are three entrances to the Annex. The northwest entrance is located under the porte-
cochère and consists of a simple, half-round arch accessed by brick steps. The northeast
entrance consists of a paneled wood door with a semicircular light, sheltered under a shed-
roofed porch with simple wood posts, a dentil cornice, and wood trellis panels. It is accessed by
concrete steps flanked by brick planters. The southeast entrance consists of a wood door
sheltered under a metal awning supported on decorative iron supports. There is a projecting
water heater shed on the southwest façade.

 4.0 CHARACTER-DEFINING FEATURES AND CONDITIONS
INVENTORY
Every historic building is unique, with its own identity and its own distinctive character.
Character-defining features are those visual aspects and physical features or elements,
constructed during the property’s period of significance, that give the building its historic
character and contribute to its historic integrity. Character-defining features should be
considered in the planning and design of a project and preserved to the maximum extent
possible. Character-defining features can identify the building as an example of a specific
building type, usually related to the building’s function; they can exemplify the use of specific
materials or methods of construction, or embody an historical period or architectural style; and
they can convey the sense of time and place in buildings associated with significant events or
people.

In general, retaining character-defining features preserves the integrity of a historic property
and maintains its eligibility as a historical resource. Removal or alteration of one feature does
not necessarily change the eligibility of a historical resource; significant impacts result from
major change, or many incremental changes over time.

Extant exterior character-defining features of the Mt. Ada Annex are identified in the table on
the following pages. The features are identified as being of either primary or secondary
significance. Although the Annex is ancillary to the Main Residence and therefore is itself of
secondary significance within the overall complex, the Annex’s features have been categorized
as primary or secondary in relation to the Annex. These determinations were made upon close
observation and were verified by cross-referencing historic photographs and other available
documentation. Spaces and features of primary significance are those that date from the period
of significance and contribute substantially to the building’s historic character. Removal or
alteration of any features of primary significance could result in a substantial loss of historic
integrity. Spaces and features of secondary significance are those that date from the period of
significance but are not critical to convey the building’s historic character; their removal or
alteration may not substantially impact the building’s historic integrity.

The table also includes an assessment of the physical condition of each feature. Conditions are
categorized as good, fair, and poor. The term good, as used in this report, means that the feature
appears sound and well maintained, and may need only minor rehabilitation. The term fair, as
used in this report, means that the feature shows a degree of disrepair and neglect, and needs
rehabilitation. The term poor, as used in this report, means that the feature is deteriorated and
needs substantial rehabilitation or replacement.
